subject: Teaching Methodology
summary: Covers assessment concepts (measurement vs evaluation; assessment of, for and as learning), formative, summative, diagnostic and placement assessment, CCE under the RTE Act and NEP 2020 reforms, test items and item analysis, qualities of a good test, and evaluation tools such as rubrics, portfolios, checklists and anecdotal records. Questions on formative assessment features, peer assessment and item types appear regularly.

sections.heading: Measurement, assessment and evaluation
sections.body:
- **Test** – an instrument or set of tasks used to obtain a sample of behaviour.
- **Measurement** – assigning numbers to attributes according to rules (e.g. 34 out of 50). It is quantitative only.
- **Assessment** – the process of gathering and interpreting evidence about learning, using tests and many other tools (observation, projects, portfolios).
- **Evaluation** – a broader process that includes quantitative and qualitative description **plus a value judgement** about worth or quality, related to objectives.
Gronlund summarised it as: Evaluation = Measurement (quantitative description) and/or non-measurement (qualitative description) + value judgement.
**Evaluation triangle**: educational objectives, learning experiences and evaluation are interlinked; each influences the others.
Purposes of assessment: diagnose learning difficulties, give feedback, improve teaching, certify achievement, guide and place students, and motivate learners.

sections.heading: Assessment of, for and as learning
sections.body:
- **Assessment of learning** – summative; measures what has been learned at the end, for grading and certification.
- **Assessment for learning** – formative; evidence is used during teaching to adjust instruction and give feedback so learners improve.
- **Assessment as learning** – learners monitor and reflect on their own learning (self-assessment, metacognition); the student is the assessor.
NCF 2005 and NEP 2020 both call for a shift from rote-based summative examinations towards regular, formative, competency-based assessment that tests higher-order skills such as analysis, critical thinking and conceptual clarity.

sections.heading: Formative, summative, diagnostic and placement
sections.body:
The terms **formative** and **summative evaluation** were introduced by **Michael Scriven (1967)** for programme evaluation; Benjamin Bloom applied them to student learning.
**Formative assessment**: conducted at regular intervals during instruction, often on an informal basis; includes questioning, observation, quizzes, self- and peer-assessment; it is **diagnostic and remedial** in nature, low-stakes and feedback-oriented.
**Summative assessment**: at the end of a unit, term or course; formal, graded, used for certification and promotion; high-stakes.
**Diagnostic assessment**: identifies specific, persistent learning difficulties and their causes, followed by **remedial teaching**.
**Placement assessment**: done before instruction to determine entry behaviour/prerequisite knowledge (e.g. a pre-test).

sections.heading: Approaches: teacher-led, self, peer and computer-based
sections.body:
**Teacher-led assessment** – the teacher designs and judges tasks (questions, tests, observation).
**Learner self-assessment** – the learner judges his/her own work against criteria or a rubric; develops metacognition and responsibility.
**Peer assessment** – classmates assess the response and performance of a learner using agreed criteria; builds critical judgement and communication. In CS, code review by peers is a natural form.
**Computer-based assessment (CBA)** – online quizzes and tests with automatic scoring and instant feedback; adaptive tests change difficulty according to responses.
**Characteristics of effective feedback**: timely; specific and descriptive (what was done well, what to improve and how); focused on the task, not the person; actionable; given in a supportive tone. Marks alone carry little information for improvement.
**Remedial teaching** follows diagnosis: re-teaching with new methods and examples, extra practice, peer tutoring and individual attention.

sections.heading: Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation (CCE)
sections.body:
The **RTE Act, 2009, Section 29(2)(h)** requires the academic authority to provide for **comprehensive and continuous evaluation** of the child's understanding of knowledge and ability to apply it.
- **Continuous** – assessment is spread throughout the session (regular formative and periodic summative), not a single final exam.
- **Comprehensive** – covers both **scholastic** areas (subjects) and **co-scholastic** areas (life skills, attitudes, values, health and physical education, arts, co-curricular activities).
Under CBSE's CCE scheme (now discontinued) formative assessments carried 40% and summative assessments 60% of the weight, and grades rather than marks were reported.
**NEP 2020** reforms: assessment that is regular, formative and competency-based; a **360-degree Holistic Progress Card (HPC)** including self- and peer-assessment; board exams that test core capacities, with an option of taking them twice a year; and **PARAKH** (Performance Assessment, Review, and Analysis of Knowledge for Holistic Development) as the national assessment centre.
**No-detention**: RTE Section 16 originally barred holding back any child until completion of elementary education; the **RTE (Amendment) Act, 2019** allows regular examinations in Classes 5 and 8 and permits detention if a child fails the re-examination, at the discretion of the appropriate government.

sections.heading: Types of test items
sections.body:
**Objective-type items** have a single correct answer and are scored without the scorer's personal judgement:
- **Selection (recognition) type**: multiple choice (stem + options: one key and distractors), true/false (alternate response), matching, assertion–reason.
- **Supply (recall) type**: fill in the blank (completion), very short answer.
**Subjective-type items**: short answer and **essay** – **restricted response** (limited scope, length) and **extended response** (freedom to organise ideas; tests higher-order thinking).
**Closed-ended items** have one definite correct answer (e.g. "Which device is called the brain of the computer?"). **Open-ended items** allow many acceptable answers (e.g. "Suggest different ways to store a list of student names", "Name as many input devices as you can").

sections.heading: Item analysis: difficulty and discrimination
sections.body:
After a test, each item is analysed to improve it.
**Steps**: score and arrange the scripts in descending order; take the top 27% as the **upper group** and the bottom 27% as the **lower group** (T.L. Kelley's 27% rule); count correct answers in each group (RU, RL).
**Difficulty index (P)** – proportion of students answering correctly. A higher P means an **easier** item. Items with P roughly between 0.25 and 0.75 (some books say 0.30–0.70) are generally retained.
**Discrimination index (D)** – how well an item separates high scorers from low scorers. D ranges from −1 to +1. Commonly cited guide (after Ebel): D ≥ 0.40 very good; 0.30–0.39 reasonably good; 0.20–0.29 marginal, needs improvement; below 0.20 poor, reject or revise. A **negative** D (lower group does better) signals a faulty item or wrong key.
**Distractor analysis**: a good distractor attracts more students from the lower group than the upper group; a distractor that nobody chooses is non-functional and should be replaced.

diagram.title: Item analysis flow
diagram.ascii:
Score all scripts -> sort high to low
        |
  top 27% = Upper (RU)   bottom 27% = Lower (RL)
        |
  P = (RU + RL) / (NU + NL)
  D = (RU - RL) / N_one_group
        |
  check distractors -> keep / revise / reject

sections.heading: Qualities of a good test
sections.body:
- **Validity** – the test measures what it intends to measure. Types: **content** (covers the syllabus and objectives in proportion), **construct** (measures the theoretical trait), **criterion-related** – **concurrent** (agrees with a present criterion) and **predictive** (predicts future performance); **face validity** (appears suitable to the taker).
- **Reliability** – consistency of scores. Methods: **test–retest** (stability), **parallel/equivalent forms**, **split-half** (corrected by the Spearman–Brown formula), **Kuder–Richardson** and Cronbach's alpha (internal consistency), **inter-rater** reliability.
- **Objectivity** – scores do not depend on who marks the test.
- **Usability/practicability** – time, cost, ease of administration and scoring.
- **Discriminating power** and appropriate **norms**.
Key relationship: a valid test must be reliable, but a reliable test need not be valid. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity.
**Blueprint (table of specifications)**: a two-way chart of **content units × objectives** (and item types), showing marks allotted to each cell. It ensures content validity and balance.

sections.heading: Norm-referenced and criterion-referenced tests
sections.body:
- **Norm-referenced test (NRT)** – interprets a student's score by comparing it with others (a norm group); gives ranks and percentiles; used for selection (e.g. entrance and recruitment exams). Items of moderate difficulty with high discrimination are preferred.
- **Criterion-referenced test (CRT)** – interprets performance against a fixed standard or set of learning outcomes ("can convert binary to decimal: yes/no"); used for mastery learning and diagnosis.
- **Achievement test** measures what has been learned; **aptitude test** predicts future learning ability; **diagnostic test** locates specific weaknesses.
- **Standardised tests** have fixed procedures, established reliability, validity and norms; **teacher-made tests** are built for a particular class.
**Grading**: **absolute grading** uses fixed score ranges (e.g. 91–100 = A1); **relative grading** assigns grades by position in the group (curve).
**Percentile rank** – the percentage of students scoring below a given score.

sections.heading: Evaluation tools and techniques
sections.body: Beyond paper-pencil tests, teachers use many tools, especially for co-scholastic areas and process skills.

sections.heading: Rubrics, portfolios and practical assessment in CS
sections.body:
**Rubric**: a scoring guide with **criteria** (rows) and **performance levels** (columns) with descriptors. **Analytic rubrics** score each criterion separately (diagnostic, detailed feedback); **holistic rubrics** give one overall score (faster, less feedback). Sharing rubrics in advance makes expectations transparent and supports self- and peer-assessment.
**Portfolio**: a purposeful collection of student work over time with reflections – e.g. programs, flowcharts, screenshots and debugging logs. **Process (working) portfolios** show growth; **showcase portfolios** show best work.
**Assessing CS practicals**: correctness of output; logic and efficiency; code readability (naming, indentation, comments); testing with boundary cases; documentation (practical file); viva voce to confirm understanding and authorship.
**Good practice**: align assessment with objectives (constructive alignment); assess process as well as product; use varied tools; give feedback before grades; avoid comparison and labelling.

formulas.name: Difficulty index
formulas.note: RU, RL = correct in upper and lower groups; NU, NL = sizes of the groups. Higher P = easier item.

formulas.name: Discrimination index
formulas.note: N₁ = number of students in one group (upper = lower). Range −1 to +1.

formulas.name: Spearman–Brown (split-half)
formulas.note: Corrects split-half correlation to full-test reliability.

formulas.name: Evaluation (Gronlund)
formulas.formula: Evaluation = Measurement / qualitative description + value judgement

workedExamples.problem: A test is given to 60 students. Upper and lower groups of 16 each are formed. For item 7, 12 students in the upper group and 4 in the lower group answer correctly. Find P and D and decide whether to keep the item.
workedExamples.solution:
- P = (RU + RL) ÷ (NU + NL) = (12 + 4) ÷ (16 + 16) = 16 ÷ 32 = **0.50** (50%) → moderate difficulty, ideal.
- D = (RU − RL) ÷ N₁ = (12 − 4) ÷ 16 = 8 ÷ 16 = **0.50** → very good discrimination (≥ 0.40).
- Decision: **retain** the item.

workedExamples.problem: For an item, RU = 5 and RL = 9 with 20 students in each group. Interpret.
workedExamples.solution:
- P = (5 + 9) ÷ 40 = 14 ÷ 40 = 0.35 → fairly difficult.
- D = (5 − 9) ÷ 20 = −4 ÷ 20 = **−0.20** → negative discrimination.
- The lower group did better: the key may be wrong or the item ambiguous. **Check the key and revise or reject** the item.

workedExamples.problem: The correlation between odd and even halves of a test is 0.60. Find the reliability of the whole test.
A 40-mark unit test must give 30% weight to knowledge, 40% to understanding and 30% to application. How many marks go to each in the blueprint?
workedExamples.solution:
- Knowledge: 30% of 40 = 0.30 × 40 = **12 marks**
- Understanding: 40% of 40 = 0.40 × 40 = **16 marks**
- Application: 30% of 40 = 0.30 × 40 = **12 marks**
- Check: 12 + 16 + 12 = 40.

workedExamples.problem: Identify the type of assessment: (a) students exchange their Python programs and comment using a rubric; (b) the teacher ends the period with a two-question exit slip to decide tomorrow's revision; (c) the term-end practical exam marks are entered in the report card.
workedExamples.solution:
- (a) Classmates judge each other's work → **peer assessment** (a form of assessment for learning).
- (b) Evidence used to adjust teaching → **formative assessment**.
- (c) End-of-term graded result → **summative assessment** (assessment of learning).

pitfalls: Measurement is only quantitative; evaluation adds qualitative description and value judgement.
Formative assessment is diagnostic and remedial and includes self- and peer-assessment; it is not limited to formal tests.
A higher difficulty index means an easier item, not a harder one.
Negative discrimination means the lower group outperformed the upper group: check the key or the item.
Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity; a reliable test can still be invalid.
A blueprint ensures content validity, not reliability.
Checklist = yes/no presence; rating scale = degree; rubric = criteria with level descriptors.
Open-ended items allow many answers; closed-ended items have one definite answer.
CCE in the RTE Act is Section 29(2)(h); no-detention was Section 16 (amended in 2019).
Norm-referenced tests compare with other students; criterion-referenced tests compare with a fixed standard.
Peer assessment means classmates assess the learner; self-assessment means the learner assesses own work.
quickRevision: Formative and summative terms: Michael Scriven (1967).
Assessment for learning = formative; of learning = summative; as learning = self-reflection.
Formative assessment: regular, informal, diagnostic and remedial, includes self and peer appraisal.
Diagnostic test is followed by remedial teaching.
CCE: continuous (throughout the year) + comprehensive (scholastic and co-scholastic).
RTE Section 29(2)(h) mandates comprehensive and continuous evaluation.
NEP 2020: Holistic Progress Card; PARAKH as national assessment centre.
Objective items: selection (MCQ, T/F, matching) and supply (completion, short answer).
Kelley: upper and lower 27% groups for item analysis.
D ≥ 0.40 very good; below 0.20 poor (Ebel's guide).
Validity: content, construct, criterion (concurrent, predictive), face.
Reliability: test–retest, parallel forms, split-half (Spearman–Brown), KR, inter-rater.
Blueprint = content × objectives table of specifications.
